title: Anthropic cuts Claude access across mainland China, Hong Kong, Macau, and Russia
subtitle: The regional policy update takes effect November 12 and covers Claude.ai, Claude Code, Cowork, APIs, and distribution through cloud resellers. Entities controlled from the restricted regions are blocked worldwide, and their personnel are blocked even when physically elsewhere.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Anthropic updated its supported-regions policy effective November 12, removing mainland China, Hong Kong, Macau, and Russia from the list of regions where Claude may be used. The restriction covers direct products — Claude.ai, Claude Code, and Cowork — and also reaches APIs, developer platforms, and Claude model services delivered through cloud service providers and authorized distributors. The policy extends to entities controlled from any of the restricted regions, and bars personnel associated with such entities from using Claude even when they are physically located in a supported region. Anthropic cites legal, regulatory, and security risks. The November change builds on an ownership-based rule introduced in September 2025 that blocked companies with at least 50 percent Chinese ownership, and on a June 2026 action against Alibaba-affiliated entities that Anthropic described as the largest extraction campaign it had ever detected.

The policy closes workarounds the previous version did not. Earlier rules hinged on where a company was legally headquartered; the new rule anchors on control and on the citizenship or affiliation of the people using the product. That shift mirrors how US export controls on advanced chips have evolved — the September 2025 and October 2026 Commerce updates moved from entity lists toward end-use and end-user criteria. Anthropic is now operating a model-vendor compliance regime that looks a lot like the regime Nvidia, AMD, and the foundries already have to run, and its competitors can be expected to follow.

This also lands during a period when Anthropic is pressing toward an IPO with risk disclosures that institutional investors are reading carefully. A clean, publicly documented position on Chinese access is a check-box item for public-market investors and for the Treasury's AI-and-chips outbound-investment rule proposed on October 25. It is harder to monetize the Chinese enterprise market than Anthropic's competitors with Chinese cloud partners can — but for a lab whose main customers are US federal, allied-government, and Fortune 500, the trade-off has clearly moved in favor of restriction.

A takeaway for learners: the AI stack is becoming geopolitically partitioned along the same fault lines as advanced chip manufacturing, and the partitioning reaches down to end users. If you work for a multinational, or you are an individual engineer who may one day be screened against an affiliation list, the cost of ambiguity is rising. Read the supported-regions pages of the AI vendors you depend on, keep documentation of your own corporate relationships current, and assume that 'where you work' and 'who you work for' are now vendor-enforced questions, not just immigration-enforced ones.
